b: Most of us learned about the synapse as a one-way street. An action potential arrives at an axon terminal, triggering neurotransmitter to cross a narrow cleft, and receptors on the next cell respond. That picture leaves out a second, less well-studied kind of connection that was first described back in the 1950s. Electrical synapses are clusters of gap junction channels that join two neurons directly. Current flows in either direction, set only by the voltage difference between the two cells, and the junction carries slow subthreshold signals along with spikes. In the mammalian brain, they mostly couple inhibitory neurons. They have stayed in the background largely because of technical challenges; detecting one requires the challenging task of simultaneously recording from two connected cells.

If you are interested in understanding more about electrical synapses, the thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN) is the natural place to look. This thin shell of GABAergic neurons wraps around the thalamus and regulates what is relayed to the cortex, which is why Francis Crick proposed it as the brain’s searchlight of attention. TRN neurons appear to make no chemical synapses with one another, so electrical synapses carry most of the communication within the reticular nucleus itself. Almost everything we know about them, however, comes from juvenile tissue. Once an animal opens its eyes, the region becomes densely packed with myelinated fibres, and paired recordings become close to impossible. Some take the silence as evidence that electrical synapses are a developmental scaffold that fades with maturity.

Julie Haas, associate professor of biological sciences at Lehigh University, found an ingenious way around the problem. Her group expressed a soma-targeted opsin in TRN neurons, patched a single cell, and then—like a child burning leaves in the yard with a magnifying glass—used a digital mirror device to illuminate neighboring cell bodies, one by one. When light on a neighbor changes the timing of spikes in the recorded cell, the two share an electrical synapse. The pilot that convinced her the method would work ran late one night in March 2020 in Kevin Bender’s lab at the University of California, San Francisco, hours after the city had told everyone to go home and shelter in place because of the COVID-19 pandemic.

The results of her work change several long-held assumptions, including the idea that electrical synapses are limited to development. Haas’ findings demonstrate conclusively that synapses do indeed persist into adulthood. Each TRN neuron couples to a handful of partners, at most about four. Coupling reaches well beyond 100 micrometers, more than double the span previously known. The synapses also link somatostatin-positive and somatostatin-negative cells, populations associated with the higher-order and first-order thalamic relays, respectively. If those connections hold in the intact brain, the TRN has a direct route through which two parallel streams of thalamic information can shape each other.

Here I speak with Haas about her path from playing the violin to studying single neurons, the history of the electrical synapse field, and the controls needed to trust a light-based measurement in tissue that scatters light. We also talk about plasticity. Coupled TRN neurons that fire together tend to weaken their shared synapse, and her method makes it possible to ask how a whole network of partners responds when one of them changes its behavior. Our conversation explores a class of synapse that neuroscience has been too quick to set aside, and what it will take to bring it back into view.
